title: Shinto: the way of the kami
examples: How do you pray at a Shinto shrine?

figure.label: Shinto shrines and a sacred mountain in Japan

explain.say: Shinto is the ancient native religion of Japan. It has no single founder and no single holy book. Its name means the way of the kami.

draw.text: Shinto: the way of the kami

draw.label: Ise Grand Shrine, the shrines of Kyoto and Mount Fuji

explain.say: Kami are sacred spirits or powers. They can be found in nature, in mountains, rivers, trees and rocks, and also in ancestors and great people. The sun kami, Amaterasu, is honoured at the Ise Grand Shrine.
A torii gate marks the entrance to a shrine, the line between the everyday world and sacred space. A rope called shimenawa, with zigzag paper, marks sacred trees and rocks.

draw.text: Torii: the gateway into sacred space

explain.say: Purity matters greatly in Shinto. Visitors rinse their hands and mouth with water, then at the shrine many bow twice, clap twice to call the kami, make a wish, and bow once more.

items: Bow and pass through the torii

explain.say: Shinto marks life with festivals called matsuri, the first shrine visit of the new year, and blessings for children at ages three, five and seven. Many people buy charms and write wishes on wooden plaques.

items: Matsuri | festivals with portable shrines and music
Hatsumode | first shrine visit of the new year
Ema | wishes written on wooden plaques

explain.say: Many Japanese people follow both Shinto and Buddhism. A common saying is that people are born Shinto and die Buddhist, because births and weddings often take place at shrines, and funerals at Buddhist temples.

faq.a: A torii is the gate at the entrance to a Shinto shrine, often painted bright vermilion. It marks the boundary between the ordinary world and sacred space. Fushimi Inari Shrine in Kyoto has thousands of torii in long tunnels.
asks: What is the red gate in Japan?

faq.a: Kami are the sacred spirits or powers honoured in Shinto. They can live in mountains, rivers, trees and rocks, in forces like wind and thunder, and in ancestors and great people. They are respected rather than feared.
asks: Do Shinto followers believe in gods?

faq.q: How do you pray at a Shinto shrine?
faq.a: First purify yourself by rinsing your hands and mouth at the water basin. At the shrine, many people toss a coin, bow twice, clap twice, pray silently, and bow once more. Customs can differ slightly between shrines.
asks: What do you do at a Shinto shrine?
Why do people clap at shrines?

faq.q: What is the difference between a shrine and a temple in Japan?
faq.a: In Japan, shrines are Shinto and honour the kami; you usually enter through a torii gate. Temples are Buddhist and honour the Buddha, often with statues and incense. Many people visit both.
asks: Is a shrine Shinto or Buddhist?

faq.a: Amaterasu is the sun kami, one of the most important kami in Shinto. In Japanese myth, the imperial family traces its line to her. Her main shrine is the Ise Grand Shrine.
asks: Who is the sun goddess of Japan?

faq.q: Does Shinto have a holy book?
faq.a: Shinto has no single holy book like the Bible or Quran. Two ancient chronicles, the Kojiki of 712 CE and the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, record the myths of the kami and the creation of Japan.

faq.q: Why is purity important in Shinto?
faq.a: Shinto teaches that impurity, called kegare, separates people from the kami, so purification, harae, restores harmony. That is why visitors wash their hands and mouth, and priests wave a purifying wand.
asks: Why do people wash at shrines?

faq.q: Why is the Ise Grand Shrine rebuilt every 20 years?
faq.a: The main buildings of Ise Grand Shrine are rebuilt every 20 years in a ceremony called Shikinen Sengu, carried on for more than a thousand years. It keeps the shrine fresh and pure and passes on the old building skills.

A matsuri is a Shinto festival. People carry the kami through the streets in portable shrines called mikoshi, with drums, music, dancing, food stalls and fireworks, to thank the kami and pray for good harvests and health.

faq.q: Can you be Shinto and Buddhist at the same time?
faq.a: Yes. Many Japanese people take part in both. Shinto shrines often celebrate births, new year and weddings, and Buddhist temples often hold funerals, so people say born Shinto, die Buddhist.
asks: Do Japanese people follow two religions?

faq.a: Omamori are small charms sold at shrines for protection, health, study or safe travel. Ema are small wooden plaques where visitors write wishes or prayers and hang them up for the kami.
asks: What are wishing plaques at shrines?

faq.q: Why are there fox statues at some shrines?
faq.a: Foxes, kitsune, are messengers of Inari, the kami of rice, harvest and prosperity. Inari shrines, like Fushimi Inari in Kyoto, have many fox statues, often holding a key or a jewel.
A shimenawa is a thick rope of rice straw, often hung with zigzag white paper streamers called shide. It marks something as sacred or pure, like a shrine gate, a giant tree or a special rock.
asks: What is the rope at Shinto shrines?

facts: Shinto means the way of the kami.
The Kojiki (712 CE) and Nihon Shoki (720 CE) record the myths of the kami.
The Ise Grand Shrine is dedicated to the sun kami Amaterasu and is rebuilt every 20 years.
Fushimi Inari Shrine in Kyoto is famous for its thousands of torii gates.
